title: BenchMint: From Real-World Tasks to Executable Benchmarks
comment: Supplementary analysis and reproducibility materials are included as ancillary files
summary: Large language models (LLMs) need evaluations of everyday reasoning and tool use, such as planning itineraries under user constraints and grounding numerical answers in evidence. We introduce BenchMint, an automated benchmark-construction workflow, and Daily-Life, its collection of 100 selected tasks across 11 real-world domains. BenchMint jointly constructs tasks and scoring criteria from the same source documents. Language-model judges assess possible answers against these criteria using tool traces and private evidence. We report 26 model/harness configurations, including GPT, Claude and Gemini families; 17 have complete domain profiles. These are descriptive configuration results, not a controlled model ranking. In one selected travel task, we corrected the reference total from 320 to 380 minutes while keeping both answers unchanged. The incorrect answer's arithmetic verdict switched from pass to fail; the correct answer's switched from fail to pass. With one ballot per cell, this exposes a reference error without establishing repeatability or collection-wide validity. Incomplete construction comparisons establish no general advantage of joint authoring or feedback-guided revision.

title: BQDNA: Multi-Head Binary Spherical Quantization for Genomic Sequence Modeling
summary: Decoding biological information from long, repetitive DNA remains challenging. Genomic language models (gLMs) often follow the conventional language-model pretrain-and-adapt paradigm. However, the lack of inherent semantic segmentation and prior rules makes hand-crafted tokenizers like k-mer and BPE suboptimal. We introduce context-aware \textbf{BQVAE} for scalar quantization of DNA and \textbf{BQDNA}, an autoregressive gLM supporting multi-head codebooks. Comprehensive experiments reveal that: (1) unique training dynamics of vector quantization in DNA space, including the importance of alignment between training corpus and downstream data. (2) superior performance of BQVAE over hand-crafted tokenizers and vanilla VQVAE. (3) remarkable cross-species generalization capability of BQDNA, which achieves state-of-the-art performance with merely 0.1B multi-species training for BQVAE and 1 epoch training on hg38 for BQDNA, outperforming gLMs pretrained with 10$\sim$100x more tokens. Our findings underscore the potential of learned vector quantization for genomic sequence representation. Code is available at https://github.com/Sophie10001b/BQDNA

title: HKD-ACPA: Heterogeneous Knowledge Distillation Adversarial Cyber-Physical Attacks in Power Grids
summary: Learning-based algorithms assist power-grid control centers in localizing transmission-line attacks, yet existing adversarial attacks typically require white-box access or repeated online queries. We study a practical zero-query setting in which an adversary coordinates physical, denial-of-service (DoS), and false data injection (FDI) attacks using only local measurements and historical detector outputs. To bridge the input-view asymmetry between local adversarial observations and DoS-masked control-center measurements, we propose Heterogeneous Knowledge Distillation Adversarial Cyber-Physical Attacks (HKD-ACPA). HKD-ACPA distills historical detector predictions into a heterogeneous graph surrogate ensemble and trains a residual calibration module to correct the view-induced logit discrepancy. Over this calibrated surrogate, we formulate sparse, magnitude-bounded FDI synthesis with a group-balanced objective that jointly induces missed detections and false alarms, and solve the resulting hybrid discrete--continuous problem via bi-level projected gradient-based proximal policy optimization (PGPPO). Experiments on the IEEE 30-bus and 118-bus systems show that HKD-ACPA outperforms all surrogate-based baselines across every sparsity budget and surpasses online-query attacks in eight of ten system--budget settings without querying the detector model.

title: Optimal Bandits with Switching Costs: $(T/\log(T))^{2/3}$ Regret
RumiFold: Teaching an LLM to Natively Fold Proteins and Reason About Their Function
summary: Can we teach a general-purpose language model to fold proteins? And if so, what does learning to fold enable beyond structure prediction itself? We introduce RumiFold, a pretrained chat model that learns to predict protein structures directly from its own hidden states. RumiFold processes proteins through repeated folding passes, then uses these folded representations to answer questions in natural language. It achieves folding accuracy comparable to dedicated single-representation models such as SimpleFold, alongside state-of-the-art performance on Gene Ontology protein function prediction and free-text function description. We find that folding pretraining organizes the model's hidden states around protein function, creating an internal per-residue workspace that is biologically grounded. Causal interventions show that this folded workspace links structure and language when RumiFold predicts function, providing rich representations for biomolecular reasoning. We see RumiFold as a step toward native biomolecular intelligence: where protein-based computations and language-based reasoning become integrated capabilities of general-purpose language models. Code, data, and models are available at: https://rumifold.baulab.info

title: Beyond Accuracy: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Hypothesis-Driven Experiment Planning in LLM Agents
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Evaluations and Datasets Track. 41 pages, 6 figures. Project website: https://schwallergroup.github.io/beyond-accuracy/
summary: Evaluating large language model (LLM) agents on scientific tasks typically reduces to final-task accuracy, which obscures where reasoning succeeds or breaks down. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic evaluation framework for hypothesis-driven adaptive experimental planning in closed-world system identification, instantiated in kinetic mechanism identification. The framework goes beyond final accuracy in two ways. First, we evaluate exploration behavior by quantifying the extent to which agents exhibit space-filling or corner-seeking patterns in the experimental design space. Second, we decompose the reasoning process into four interpretable steps: belief update, hypothesis discrimination, discriminative experiment design, and predictive reasoning under interventions, each scored separately on reasoning traces. Across ten LLM agents, we find that stronger agents outperform both adaptive (Bayesian optimization) and non-adaptive (Latin hypercube) baselines and exhibit exploration patterns inconsistent with naive heuristics. Decomposing reasoning reveals that the stronger agents score consistently well across all four steps, whereas weaker agents often succeed at belief update and hypothesis discrimination but are less reliable at translating them into actionable designs and sharp contrastive predictions. Independent expert annotations support predictive reasoning under our stated validation criteria, while evidence for discriminative experiment design is positive but less consistent. The results suggest a gap between recognizing plausible hypotheses and translating them into contrastive predictions, with more tentative evidence for a corresponding experiment-design bottleneck. The benchmark website is available at https://schwallergroup.github.io/beyond-accuracy/.

title: OnCache: Learning Dynamic Caching Schedules for Efficient Diffusion Inference
summary: Diffusion models have revolutionized generative tasks but incur high inference latency due to iterative denoising. Cache-based strategies accelerate inference by reusing intermediate features, yet they largely rely on static, sample-agnostic schedules. Our empirical analysis reveals two factors that these schedules overlook. (i) denoising dynamics and computational requirements vary across prompts, motivating adaptive computation allocation. (ii) sensitivity to caching errors varies across timesteps, so static schedules may reuse features at error-sensitive steps or waste computation at less sensitive ones. We therefore propose OnCache, a dynamic caching framework that makes prompt-adaptive decisions online about how much computation to allocate and when to refresh cached features. A policy is trained offline on paired compute and cache continuations from identical denoising states, using differences in terminal fidelity and the number of function evaluations (NFE) to account for the downstream consequences of each decision. To further improve the generation quality, a neural corrector compensates for caching-induced errors and mitigates their accumulation throughout the denoising trajectory. Both components are lightweight and introduce negligible additional inference latency. On FLUX.1-dev, OnCache achieves a nearly $3\times$ generation speedup at $1024^2$ resolution, with LPIPS of $0.156$ and SSIM of $0.860$. We further extend OnCache to video generation on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, achieving state-of-the-art efficiency--quality trade-offs across both modalities.

title: Vanishing Initialization Turns Diagonal Tensor Gradient Flow into Greedy Matching
summary: We study gradient-flow (GF) learning of tensors from vanishing initialization in canonical polyadic (CP) factorization models. For tensors of order $ν\geq3$ whose targets are diagonal in mode-wise orthonormal bases, we prove that the limiting learning dynamics follows a simple greedy bipartite matching process. Each rank-one component of the model, called an atom, can potentially learn each rank-one component of the target, called a scalar sector. Every atom--sector pair has an initialization-dependent activation clock, representing the time at which the atom would grow to macroscopic size in that sector if the pair evolved in isolation. Processing these clocks in increasing order and selecting a pair whenever neither its atom nor its sector has been selected before determines the sequence of actual learning events. We prove that the GF trajectory converges to the corresponding staircase of learned target components. The task of learning modular addition by a CP model with complex weights falls exactly into this framework after Fourier diagonalization. Its activation clocks are independent and identically distributed, allowing us to combine the GF reduction with known random matching asymptotics and derive an explicit, distribution-free large-system loss curve after time reparametrization. We also obtain an asymptotic formula relating this curve to the original GF training time. For models with real weights, conjugate Fourier modes instead form two-dimensional blocks with richer internal structure. We characterize their rank and border-rank cascade and conjecture that the corresponding GF dynamics follows interleaved multi-stage learning processes.

title: Learning Global Probabilistic Explanations
summary:
Interpreting the predictions of complex black-box classifiers remains a central challenge in explainable artificial intelligence.
  While local explanations clarify individual predictions, there is a significant need for global probabilistic explanations that capture a model's overall behavior across the input distribution.
  Such an explanation is a small subset $K$ of features, whose relevance is measured by the expected probability, over a random input $\mathbf x$, that the classifier assigns the same label to $\mathbf x$ and to a random input agreeing with $\mathbf x$ on $K$.
  In this study, we investigate the task of identifying maximally relevant global explanations under a cardinality constraint, focusing on product distributions with full support on discrete feature spaces.
  We introduce a spectral explainer that leverages membership queries to the black-box classifier and employs Fourier-analytic, junta-learning methods to produce probably approximately correct (PAC) explanations.
  Our algorithm is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the explanation size limit, maximum feature cardinality, and desired accuracy.
  Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the theoretical guarantees and show that the spectral explainer outperforms a greedy baseline as the explanation size increases.

title: CoHABIT: Complementary Evaluation of Furniture Layouts through Spatial Rules and Household Routines
summary: We introduce CoHABIT, a framework for evaluating furniture layouts through complementary spatial rules and household routines. Static assessment captures geometric validity, ergonomic access, functional organization, and configurable design preferences, including Feng Shui. Dynamic assessment uses learned resident policies to simulate everyday activities, resource sharing, coordination, and individual burdens in multi-agent households. Controlled comparisons show how spatial criteria and household behavior reveal distinct aspects of layout quality, while resident profiles and scheduling influence furnishing rankings. Independent verification of household needs grounds dynamic comparisons in observed outcomes, enabling interpretable assessments of how furnished environments serve different households.

title: GeoFusion: An Uncertain Machine Learning Framework for Sensor Fusion
summary: High positioning precision is a critical requirement in many Global Positioning System (GPS) applications, yet achieving it with affordable smartphone sensors remains an open challenge. Existing approaches treat each GPS observation as an absolute point, discarding the uncertainty inherent in the measurement conditions and leaving the cooperative potential of multiple phones observing the same location untapped. In this work, we propose GeoFusion, a three-stage uncertain machine learning framework for cooperative sensor fusion. In the first stage, each GPS observation is modeled as an uncertain object using one of two proposed models: the volcano function, grounded in satellite geometry, and the empirically derived mountain function, built from the statistical structure of real smartphone data. In the second stage, uncertain objects are clustered by location event using partitional and graph-based algorithms. In the third stage, the cluster output is refined using filter-based and learning-based estimators. Experiments on the Google Smartphone Decimeter Challenge dataset show that uncertainty modeling is a primary driver of precision gains: the mountain function significantly outperforms the geometry-only volcano function, and uncertainty-aware UK-medoids significantly outperforms its certain counterpart, k-medoids. A post-clustering deep neural network further refines the cluster estimates, and the recommended configuration achieves a mean absolute error of 2.90 +/- 0.15 meters on held-out test drives, comparable to and on average below the best reported single-phone precision of approximately 3 meters, demonstrating the potential of cooperative uncertainty-aware fusion for affordable GPS sensors.

title: Recursive Self-Editing: LLMs Program Their Own Weight Edits for Self-Improvement
summary: Recursive self-improvement asks a system to improve the very system that improves it. Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. We let the model write its own weights. In SELFWRITE, each generation the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives (singular directions, activation contrasts between its right and wrong answers, rank-one projections, tensor computations), with no training or gradient tool. Every candidate is graded once on a hidden gate set against the current model; the best strictly improving edit is merged into the weights, and the edited model writes the next edit. On Qwen3.8-27B and math problems from DAPO-Math, five generations of SELFWRITE raise gate accuracy from 73.95% to 76.45% and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees from 76.30% to 77.75% (avg@4) and from 82.60% to 84.80% (pass@4), without a single gradient step. A language model can author useful changes to its own weights without gradients, and the edited model keeps writing useful edits.

title: Adaptation or Poisoning? Security Risks of Conversational Test-Time Learning in Large Language Models
summary: Test-time learning (TTL) enables large language models to adapt to unlabeled inputs during deployment. The model updates a lightweight adapter by minimizing the next-token prediction loss on the input it receives. When these updates persist across conversation turns, every user query serves both as the request answered in the current turn and as adaptation data for later turns. By choosing the queries used for adaptation, an attacker can influence parameter updates and weaken safety alignment through ordinary interactions with a TTL chat service. To demonstrate this risk, we introduce Progressive Test-Time Adaptation Poisoning (P-TAP), a query-only multi-turn attack that jailbreaks the model by poisoning its session adapter through the service's own updates. A sequence of escalating adversarial queries shapes the adapter turn by turn; the final harmful request is then answered under the accumulated state without itself being used for adaptation. Across four open-weight instruction-tuned models, enabling updates raises attack success rates on average by 13.00 percentage points under greedy decoding and by 22.25 points under best-of-10 sampling, relative to matched sessions receiving the same queries without updates. Answering adversarial queries but adapting on unrelated text or on benign text about the same topic removes most of this increase. Among existing safeguards, screening incoming queries flags every attack stream before the final request, while a perplexity-based detector of unsafe adaptation flags none of the successful attacks.

title: Learning Acceptable Lotteries via Queries: Minimizing Aggregated Violation Distances
summary: When deploying an AI system, a developer can randomize over several candidate versions, sending each request to a version chosen at random, to balance the requirements of multiple stakeholders. We study a setting in which each of $n$ stakeholders reveals only whether a proposed lottery over $m$ candidates is acceptable, and each stakeholder's acceptable lotteries lie on one side of an unknown hyperplane. While previous work sought a lottery that every stakeholder accepts, such a lottery need not exist when, for instance, safety and helpfulness requirements are in conflict. We therefore minimize a power mean of the stakeholders' violations; since binary answers reveal neither the size of a violation nor how to compare violations across stakeholders, we measure each violation by a normalized distance to the stakeholder's acceptance boundary. We characterize exactly when accept/reject answers determine these distances. When they do, $\mathcal{O}(nm\log(1/\varepsilon))$ queries suffice to learn them, where $\varepsilon$ is the precision of the utilities, and this bound is tight; when they do not, a natural worst-case approach is optimal up to a constant factor, even compared with methods that make unlimited queries. For limited query budgets, we give a sampling algorithm whose number of queries for a given accuracy does not depend on $n$, and show that a deterministic algorithm cannot guarantee a small loss without querying almost all stakeholders. Synthetic experiments illustrate the resulting tradeoff between querying many stakeholders and learning each of them accurately.

title: Think Before You Forecast: Scaling Test-Time Compute for Time Series Forecasting
summary: Test-time compute has become an important paradigm in computer vision and language modeling, where additional computation at inference time enables models to explore multiple candidate solutions and select or refine the most reliable one. However, time series forecasting models typically produce predictions through a single forward pass, leaving them vulnerable to distribution shifts and non-stationarity that frequently arise in real-world temporal data. We propose Time Test Compute for Time Series (TTC4TS), an architecture-agnostic framework that improves the predictive performance of frozen forecasting models at inference time. Given a pretrained backbone, the generator produces multiple candidate forecast trajectories using augmentation, retrieval, adapter. The synthesizer then selects or combines these candidates using aggregation, classification, or candidate-scoring and ranking methods to produce the final forecast. By increasing the number of candidates, TTC4TS scales test-time compute without retraining the forecasting backbone. Beyond improving point-forecast accuracy, TTC4TS can exploit candidate forecasts for uncertainty quantification, which supports improved interval forecasts. We also theoretically analyze when additional test-time computation improves forecasting. Experiments across diverse datasets and backbones demonstrate consistent gains in accuracy and calibration. Code is provided in https://github.com/Anoise/TTC4TS.

title: From Learning Rates to Rotational Schedules: Finite-Horizon Theory on the Sphere
summary: How should step sizes be scheduled across a finite training horizon? Cosine and warmup-stable-decay (WSD) schedules are widely adopted in large-scale pretraining, yet their effect on optimization also depends on parameter norms. Normalization can make parameter groups scale invariant, so that the loss depends only on their direction, while their norms still affect how fast the parameters rotate. In this work, we formulate schedule design directly in the space of rotational motion. Working within a geodesically convex spherical setting, we derive a last-iterate convergence guarantee for arbitrary rotational schedules that separates their overall scale from their distribution over time. We derive the unique schedule that minimizes this bound and prove that it approaches linear decay as the horizon grows. Empirically, our rotational interpretation and idealized spherical analysis provide useful predictions for LLM pretraining in practice, including schedule comparisons missed by existing analyses. Our analysis predicts schedule ordering across model scales for both vanilla (Adam, Muon) and Hyperball-style (AdamH, MuonH) optimizers. Our Hyperball experiments support the predicted strong performance of linear LR decay and confirm our prediction that WSD underperforms in this setting. Accounting for parameter norm dynamics, we predict instead the strong performance of WSD for Adam and Muon shown in practice. Guided by our theoretical insights, we also derive a new LR schedule for Adam and Muon, which improves over the established cosine and WSD schedules. All in all, these results support the use of rotational dynamics to understand, predict, and ultimately guide scheduling in LLM pretraining.

title: How Multi-Timescale Memory Cools Optimization: Theory and Evidence from AdEMAMix
summary: Augmenting AdamW with multiple momentum timescales improves large language model pretraining, yet the mechanism driving these gains remains poorly understood. We identify an interaction between multi-timescale optimizer memory and the geometry of normalized networks: memory changes parameter norms and thereby controls how fast parameters rotate. Starting from exact norm dynamics under decoupled weight decay, we show that the parameter norm depends on the temporal correlation of the updates, with weight decay controlling how long these correlations influence optimization. We show how an independently weighted slow momentum can substantially increase the norm of parameters, while contributing negligible power to the instantaneous update, therefore acting as an endogenous annealing schedule. We study this mechanism in AdEMAMix for language-model pretraining. Controlled interventions show that this scheduling mechanism has clear practical consequences and is an important factor behind AdEMAMix's advantage over AdamW.

title: Aggregation Dispersion: An Information-Geometric Diagnostic of Oversmoothing in Graph Neural Networks
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Message-passing neural networks (MPNNs) learn node representations by iteratively aggregating information from neighbors, but stacking too many layers causes all representations to converge, an effect known as oversmoothing. We propose a geometric perspective on this phenomenon. At each depth $k$, the propagation operator assigns to every node $v$ a walk distribution $p_v^{(k)}$, a probability distribution over source nodes. These walk distributions form a point cloud on the probability simplex, whose contraction to a single point characterizes complete mixing of the propagation operator, and thus oversmoothing. To measure this contraction, we use the Fisher-Rao metric, the unique Riemannian metric on the simplex invariant up to scale under sufficient statistics, whose scaled chordal distance under the square-root embedding $p \mapsto \sqrt{p}$ is the Hellinger distance. The resulting diagnostic, the aggregation dispersion $D_k$, is the variance of the embedded point cloud on the unit sphere. We prove that: (i) $D_k = 0$ if and only if the $k$-th step propagation matrix has rank one, a necessary and sufficient condition for complete operator mixing; (ii) $D_k$ is non-increasing with depth; (iii) the spectral gap of the propagation matrix controls the rate of this decay; and (iv) for contractive MPNNs, the aggregation dispersion upper-bounds the representation dispersion up to graph- and initialization-dependent constants. Across 14 model configurations and 11 datasets, $D_k$ attains the highest mean absolute Pearson correlation with test accuracy across depths among eight diagnostics ($|r| = 0.721$, using log-transformed diagnostic values), numerically comparable to the post-training effective rank ($|r| = 0.688$), while requiring no training.

title: Attacking Tabular Foundation Models: An Experimental Taxonomy of Context Poisoning and Test-Time Evasion
summary: Tabular foundation models condition predictions on labeled examples supplied at inference time, creating an attack surface that differs from conventional model training. We study four manipulation families (label flipping, backdoor context poisoning, clean-label context selection, and test-time evasion) and organize them by attack stage, label consistency, and distributional realism. TabPFN-2.5, TabICL, and XGBoost are evaluated on CIC-IDS2017 and N-BaIoT using a common preprocessing and evaluation pipeline. Backdoor context poisoning provides strong targeted control over the in-context models with little change in clean accuracy, whereas selecting real, correctly labeled boundary-crowding rows causes no systematic accuracy degradation up to a 20% bias fraction. A simplified surrogate-transfer constrained PGD attack inspired by, but not equivalent to, CAPGD also produces test-time evasion, outperforming equal-budget random noise in most settings. The comparison shows that attack effectiveness depends strongly on both where manipulation occurs and how much freedom the attacker has to alter the data.

title: How Seasonal Reference Choice Changes the Apparent Gains of Chronos Models in Electricity Load Forecasting
summary: When a forecasting model is said to beat a simple baseline, the size of that win depends on which baseline was used. We measure how much this matters for two zero-shot foundation models, Chronos-Bolt and Chronos-2, on hourly electricity load. The study uses 60 fixed cases drawn from eight series in four public collections, with forecasts 24 and 168 hours ahead and up to 2,048 hours of history. Each model is compared with daily persistence, weekly persistence, a weekday hybrid, a daily-weekly blend, and a reference chosen from these on a validation period. We keep every origin-level forecast and estimate uncertainty with paired circular block bootstrap intervals using 168- and 336-hour blocks. A week ahead, Bolt clearly beats weekly persistence in 21 of 30 cases but the validation-selected reference in only 14, and its median gain falls from 17.3% to 11.9%. For Chronos-2 the clear-win counts are 18 and 15. Chronos-2 has lower week-ahead MAE than Bolt in 24 cases, yet only 12 of those differences are clear. The selected reference is not always the harder baseline, since on some test windows it does worse than weekly persistence. The choice of baseline therefore changes both how large the reported gain is and how sure we can be of it. The results are exploratory: the series and windows are related, an earlier pilot was inspected, pretraining overlap cannot be ruled out, and the case-level intervals are not corrected for multiple comparisons.

title: One Checkpoint, Four Converters: Per Input Disagreement After On Device Conversion and a Probe Set That Catches It
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures. Also archived on Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.24433993
summary: A model converted for on device or accelerated inference ships once its top 1 accuracy matches the source model. Accuracy can match while individual decisions change, and the converter, its INT8 recipe and its calibration draw each move them. We convert 5 public checkpoints (four ImageNet classifiers and a sentiment model) with the documented FP32 and INT8 recipes of ExecuTorch, LiteRT, ONNX Runtime and TensorRT and compare every top 1 decision with the PyTorch source on 7,854 images and 1,938 sentences. All 34 strict FP32 conversions reproduce every decision, yet each of the 4 vision INT8 recipes that keeps accuracy equivalent flips more than 1% of decisions: ONNX Runtime static INT8 flips 4.07% (95% CI [3.65, 4.53]) of ResNet 50 decisions while accuracy moves by -0.15 points, and two builds of that recipe from different calibration draws disagree on 3.44% [3.06, 3.88]. Where accuracy is kept, the flipped inputs are the ones the source model barely decides (AUROC of the source margin 0.90 to 0.97 on ResNet 50, every 95% CI inside [0.89, 0.98]), but our preregistered claim that this holds for every recipe fails on the two mobile networks, where INT8 breaks accuracy outright. A probe set of the 200 training inputs with the smallest source margin, chosen before any conversion, flags all 40 vision stacks (recall 95% CI [0.91, 1.00]) and all 6 text stacks that flip at least 0.5% of decisions and none of the exact FP32 conversions, so conversion checks should compare decisions on such a probe set, not accuracy.

title: Exact on Paper: Which LLM Serving Shortcuts Flip Graded Answers, Measured Against the Noise of Reordering the Same Requests
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. Also archived on Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.24433980
summary: Teams enable serving features such as prefix caching, chunked prefill and speculative decoding after checking that benchmark accuracy is unchanged, because the engine documents them as exact. Accuracy is an aggregate, so a feature can hold it while flipping which requests are answered correctly. We serve one 4B instruction model in vLLM under nine single feature configurations and five replicas of a reference configuration, grade 3,380 requests from five benchmarks in every run, and compare each candidate with a restart floor (fresh process) and a scheduling floor (same requests in a different order). With default kernels every configuration keeps accuracy within one point, and the seven exact features flip the graded outcome of 1.47% (95% CI 1.13 to 1.85) to 1.78% (1.39 to 2.20) of requests, none above the scheduling floor of 1.72%, while the FP8 KV cache flips 3.36% (2.80 to 3.96), as many as FP8 weights. With batch invariant kernels all seven exact features, speculative decoding included, reproduce the reference text on every request, while the FP8 KV cache still flips 3.91% (3.28 to 4.53) of graded outcomes. A gate that compares against a single replica pair rejected an unchanged configuration, so we recommend certifying a serving change under batch invariant kernels, where the floor is zero, or against a scheduling floor measured from at least three replicas.

title: CrysLDM: Latent Diffusion Model for Crystal Material Generation
summary: Generating new crystal materials with desirable chemical properties has long been a challenging task. Existing diffusion models operate in feature space, requiring complex diffusion architectures to model the joint distribution of atom types, coordinates, and lattice structures. This complexity increases the number of diffusion steps, leading to higher training and sampling costs. In this work, we aim to generate novel crystal materials within a time- and resource-constrained setup, where existing models are not well-suited. To address this, we propose CrysLDM, a novel latent diffusion model for 3D crystal materials, which integrates a variational autoencoder and a diffusion model. The VAE encoder maps 3D crystal structures into a latent space, where the diffusion model operates. Since CrysLDM leverages a smooth, lower-dimensional latent space, it simplifies the generative process and accelerates both training and inference. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets and tasks, we show that CrysLDM generates stable and valid materials with quality comparable to state-of-the-art methods, while being significantly more efficient in terms of computational resources and time.

title: Towards Global Counterfactual-Based Self-Explainable Graph Neural Networks
summary: Graph Counterfactual Explanations (GCEs) have emerged as an effective approach for interpreting Graph Neural Network (GNN) predictions by identifying minimal graph modifications needed to change predictions. However, existing methods suffer from two fundamental limitations: (1) They rely on a post-hoc explanation paradigm, where a separate explainer is trained after the GNN. This sequential optimization prevents the explainer from leveraging how the GNN learned its representations, often resulting in lower-quality explanations. (2) They are largely local, generating counterfactual explanations only for individual samples. Consequently, they fail to capture generalizable patterns across the data distribution, a crucial gap for applications like drug discovery, where global principles enable systematic decision-making across thousands of cases. To address these limitations, we propose GCSGNN (Global Counterfactual-based Self-explainable GNN), a unified framework that integrates counterfactual generation into the GNN architecture, encouraging explanations that faithfully reflect the model's decision-making process. Beyond local explanations, GCSGNN discovers shared latent patterns influencing predictions across graphs, yielding global (i.e., model-level) counterfactual explanations. We further introduce an efficient latent-space counterfactual mechanism that avoids the combinatorial complexity of discrete graph manipulation, enabling scalable discovery of generalizable modification patterns. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that GCSGNN outperforms existing methods in generating effective counterfactual explanations. Our code is available at https://github.com/wendyzheng22/gcsgnn.

title: Loop-Count Schedules in Looped Transformers: An Empirical Study
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables. Code: https://github.com/kvoyager/gatedloop-transformer. Trained weights and per-token traces: https://huggingface.co/konstank/gatedloop-transformer
summary: Looped transformers apply one block of layers several times with shared weights, trading parameters for repeated computation. We study how the schedule of the loop iteration count R during training determines whether each extra pass acts as a full layer or as a small correction, using a controlled ladder of 46M-110M-parameter models trained on 2B tokens with learned residual gates on every loop pass and three schedules: R fixed to 2, R sampled uniformly from {1,...,6}, and R sampled from {2,3,4}. We find that the lower bound of the sampling range is the decisive choice. If the sampled range includes R=1, so that some training steps run the block only once and compute the loss on that single pass, the gates collapse to 0.1-0.5 and each additional pass becomes a small correction to the first; if the range starts at R=2, so that every training step runs the block at least twice, the gates stay at 0.6-0.9 and each pass keeps the strength of a full layer, while the model can still be run at any R from 2 up to twice the largest trained value with validation loss within a few hundredths of a nat of its best. The {2, 3, 4} schedule gives the best looped model, 2.909 nats against 2.951 for the parameter-matched plain model, and degrades by only 0.038 nats when run at twice its trained depth. We further show that under a fixed R the direction of the residual stream converges geometrically beyond the trained depth while the loss diverges, which refines a recent finding that static-depth training does not converge, and that reusing the first pass's keys and values on later passes costs 0.01-0.03 nats in every regime while making the per-token iteration uniformly contractive and halving the inference cache. The loop recovers about a third of what real depth provides at equal parameters. The code, trained weights, and per-token traces are released.

title: Learning-Augmented QUBO for Time-Expanded Multi-Commodity Flow
summary: We study energy-aware multi-commodity flow on time-expanded graphs, a problem that captures dynamic routing in layered networks and is NP-hard in general. We formulate the problem as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization problem, give an explicit penalty coefficient that provably guarantees feasibility, and show that it is smaller than the standard bound by a factor of roughly the number of active links. The layered structure of the time-expanded graph yields three structural results: a treewidth bound that gives a fixed-parameter tractable exact algorithm in the bag size, a matrix-product-operator representation of small bond dimension, and a proof that the annealing gap of the associated Ising Hamiltonian is strictly positive for every instance with a unique optimum, uniformly over bounded windows. For learning-augmented routing, we bound the Hamming distance between a predicted and an optimal flow by the flow error, and prove a consistency guarantee: a hybrid algorithm that keeps the better of the prediction and the solver output returns a flow whose cost exceeds the optimum by a factor that grows linearly with the prediction error. The results are exact statements about the QUBO and its associated Ising Hamiltonian, and they hold for any physical implementation.

title: From States to Dynamics: Detecting Rule Violations in OthelloGPT
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS workshop, Interpretability as a Science: Toward rigorous foundations for understanding LLMs; 20 pages, 16 figures total (including Appendix)
summary: Sequence models trained on game moves have been shown to encode world models, with structured linear probes revealing the underlying game states. World models, however, are inherently dynamic: in deterministic board games, a set of rules constrain how states evolve over time. We therefore ask if and how OthelloGPT, a transformer trained only on Othello move sequences, manifests the rules of the game in its activation space. We divide the rules of Othello, and symmetrically their violations, into three classes: placing a disc on an empty square (R1), flanking an opponent's disc (R2), and moving in turn (R3). We find that linear probes accurately separate legal from illegal moves, and also distinguish between the three kinds of rule violations. We introduce an unsupervised rule-violation detector based on the step length of activations between consecutive moves, which identifies illegal moves above chance. We further improve our detection metric by computing step length in the latent space of select sparse autoencoders. Together, we find that OthelloGPT follows game rules of Othello to a large extent, and that we can detect rule violations using structured detectors on model activations.

title: Randomized Weighted Distance Nearest Neighbor Classification
comment: Writing-polished version of the SMC'26 paper
summary: The nearest neighbor classifier is known to be memory-inefficient, and a popular solution is to compress its training data. Recently, a compression algorithm based on weighted distance nearest neighbor (WNN) was proposed, which has elegant theoretical properties and effective classification performance. However, its compression process is computationally expensive, for it performs a greedy search of the densest homogeneous balls in data space. In this paper, we propose a randomized variant RWNN. It simply randomizes the ball search process, and results in substantially reduced compression time (often 0.1%--1% of WNN's) and similar classification accuracy. RWNN also inherits several theoretical properties of WNN including consistency and a generalization bound. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate its efficacy.

title: LAF-ECG: Multi-Resolution Lead-Aware Fusion of Time-Series and Language Foundation Models for ECG Classification
summary: Automated electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation has advanced substantially with deep learning, yet many methods remain task-specific and label-dependent. Large language models (LLMs) and time-series foundation models (TSFMs) offer complementary pretrained representations, but integrating them is challenging because of mismatched feature spaces and the lead- and scale-dependent structure of ECG signals. We propose LAF-ECG (Lead-Aware Foundation Fusion for ECG), a dual-foundation framework that extends MedTsLLM with a lead-aware interface to a frozen TSFM backbone while retaining its reprogramming pathway. The proposed framework captures multi-resolution temporal context, fuses temporal and language-aligned ECG representations through adaptive residual integration, and employs branch-specific supervision with cross-branch alignment. LAF-ECG achieves 71.10% accuracy and 62.43% macro-F1 on PTB-XL, and 89.73% accuracy and 65.94% macro-F1 on Chapman-Shaoxing, outperforming MedTsLLM on both datasets. These results highlight the value of preserving lead-specific temporal structure when combining temporal and language foundation representations for ECG classification. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/kkianamm/LAF-ECG.

title: Deterministic Proper Positive-Only Learning Is Independent of ZFC
summary: Binary classification from positive-only samples is a variant of PAC learning in which the learner receives i.i.d. samples only from the positive region of an unknown target concept, but is evaluated on the full distribution. Improper learnability in this model has a textbook characterization, whereas proper learnability has remained open for decades. Recent work characterized it for learners with access to randomness, and showed that, unlike in PAC learning, some classes are properly learnable with randomness but not without it, leaving the deterministic case open. We show that this case cannot be resolved within the standard axioms of mathematics (ZFC): there is a class of VC dimension two whose deterministic proper learnability is independent of ZFC, even though a randomized learner provably learns it. Moreover, no dimension of finite character, a desirable property shared by most dimensions in learning theory, characterizes deterministic proper learnability. We also show that the size of the domain is decisive. In ZFC, deterministic proper learnability has a combinatorial characterization on every domain whose cardinality is below a certain threshold, including every countable domain. In contrast, this characterization fails on every domain of sufficiently large cardinality. Under the generalized continuum hypothesis, this threshold is sharp: it is the exact cardinality at which the characterization starts to fail. Finally, our proofs introduce new tools, based on the Erdos--Rado partition theorem, that may be of broader interest.

title: Why Units Die in the Layer After a Frozen Random Encoder, and What the Number of Live Units Measures
comment: 31 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Supplementary material (121 pages) is included as an ancillary file
summary: Reinforcement-learning agents can learn Atari games through a convolutional encoder whose random weights are never trained. They reach expert play in Pong and, without random action repeats, in Breakout, but training takes far longer and few ReLU units in the layer after the encoder stay alive. A dead unit outputs zero for every input and cannot learn. In earlier work we took the number of live units to measure the game's complexity. Here we ask why units die and correct that conclusion. We find that more units die as the layer's inputs lie farther from zero relative to how much they vary. We call this ratio the offset. Earlier work showed this in sparse autoencoders at the start of training. We saw it after training in agents, image classifiers, a reservoir computer and sparse autoencoders on GPT-2. A random encoder leaves the offset of its input roughly unchanged, and a formula predicted its median offset within 25 percent in all 44 cases. So a game with a bright, mostly unchanging screen gives the next layer a large offset. In Pong, subtracting the average screen raised the number of live units from between 3 and 6 of 64 to between 59 and 63, so the number alone cannot show a game's complexity. On unaltered screens none of the agents reached a training score of 18 in 50 million steps. With the subtraction all did within 5 million, about as fast as a trained encoder on unaltered screens. In Breakout the subtraction left more units alive, but average training scores did not clearly improve, and a large gap to a trained encoder remained. So we do not treat their number as something to raise for its own sake. The evidence is from small networks and three games, and in agents and image classifiers changing the offset also changed the size of the inputs. We suggest measuring the offset before training a layer on a fixed front end and, if it is large, trying to subtract the mean input.

title: What Should World Models Plan Over? Learning Geometry-Aligned Representations of Body Motion
summary: We introduce MotionPort, which learns low-dimensional latent representations of body motion for accurate dynamics prediction and effective long-horizon planning. Existing world-model planners often search over action representations learned for prediction, yet we show that predictive accuracy alone does not ensure that optimization can discover successful trajectories. MotionPort addresses this mismatch by representing body trajectories rather than action chunks and organizing the search space by motion similarity, helping predicted improvements translate into successful execution. Without fine-tuning state encoders, MotionPort raises average goal-reaching success from 37.9% to 87.8% across three backbones and seven settings in four domains. On the evaluated AntMaze-OGBench tasks, it achieves 72% success, compared with 4% for the strongest baseline.

title: probly: Uncertainty-Aware Machine Learning
summary: As machine learning systems are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, the question of how to represent and quantify uncertainty has moved from a methodological side issue to a central concern. In practice, however, making a model uncertainty-aware is still surprisingly difficult: relevant tools tend to be scattered across libraries, each tied to a particular framework and a particular approach to modeling uncertainty, and the choice of representation, quantification, and evaluation is typically left to the user without much guidance. In this paper, we present probly, a Python package that addresses these issues in a single, modular framework. probly offers (i) lightweight transformations that turn existing models into uncertainty-aware ones, currently supporting PyTorch, scikit-learn, and Flax, (ii) several representations, including second-order distributions, credal sets, and conformal prediction, (iii) the corresponding quantification measures, and (iv) a number of evaluation protocols, which can be combined more or less arbitrarily. Using probly, we conduct a benchmark study on three standard tasks --- selective prediction, out-of-distribution detection, and active learning. In addition, and unlike existing benchmarks, we evaluate suitable methods on first-order data, i.e., datasets for which the target itself is a distribution over outcomes. We further illustrate the flexibility of the package on a number of less standard case studies, including large language models, graph neural networks, and data streams. The package is publicly available at https://github.com/pwhofman/probly.

title: Selecting Stable Sampling Dynamics for Compositional Diffusion: A Feynman-Kac Weight Reduction
summary: Given $K$ separately trained diffusion models, how should one sample from a $β_k$-weighted product of their terminal laws without jointly retraining the experts? Existing Feynman--Kac constructions provide many weighted stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with the correct target marginal. The consequential question is how to select useful proposal dynamics among them. We study an explicit family of weighted diffusions that realizes the same product-of-intermediate-experts trajectory. A scalar parameter $λ$ controls how strongly the proposal drift follows the composed expert score, while an additional Langevin component can be varied independently. Writing $B=\sum_{k=1}^{K}β_k>0$, we identify the distinguished choice $λ=1/B$. At this value, the aggregate squared-score term in the instantaneous Feynman--Kac log-weight rate cancels exactly. For positive expert exponents, the remaining score-disagreement contribution is non-positive. We call this structural cancellation Feynman--Kac reduction. Under bounded-divergence assumptions, it yields an upper bound on the instantaneous unnormalized log-weight rate for all $λ\leq 1/B$. For linear diffusion protocols with compactly supported expert data, $λ=1/B$ yields two-sided bounds at every nonterminal time, for exponents of either sign. A corresponding result holds for a single expert under the same divergence assumption. In these two-sided settings, the selected value is unique within the specified family in a universal worst-case sense. Experiments on Gaussian mixtures and molecular sampling compare the analytically predicted stability with actual sampling quality, including instances in which parameter choices different from $λ=1/B$ perform better empirically.

title: When Simpler Beats Learned: Dual-Weighted Sampling vs. Machine Learning for the Pricing Subproblem in Graph Coloring
summary: The graph coloring problem can be solved to optimality by branch-and-price (B&P), but its performance hinges on the column generation (CG) step, where each iteration requires solving a maximum weight independent set (MWIS) pricing problem. The state-of-the-art machine-learning (ML) pricing heuristic follows a prediction-sampling paradigm: a learned model scores each vertex of a graph, and independent sets are sampled from the induced distribution. We observe, however, that the scoring procedure does not need to be learned, and critically assess the role of ML by replacing the learned scores with the dual solution of the restricted master problem, resulting in Dual-Weighted Sampling, a proposed lightweight alternative that requires no feature engineering or training. Within a unified CG and B&P framework that varies only the pricing oracle, Dual-Weighted Sampling outperforms MLPH, hand-crafted heuristics, and exact solvers on the established graph coloring benchmark in both runtime and solution quality. In particular, it remains competitive on the DIMACS random family, where MLPH was shown strongest in the original evaluation, while achieving more than a two-fold speedup in CG runtime on recursive-sparse and real-world graph families.

title: Constrained Diffusion from Binary Evaluations via Learned Doob h-Functions
summary: Conditional generation under constraints that can only be checked on a finished sample, such as a molecular property filter, remains challenging for diffusion models: most guidance methods require differentiable measurement operators, paired conditional data, or rollouts of the base model at every step. We present a framework grounded in the Doob $h$-transform that reduces conditional generation to learning a single function, the probability that a noisy sample denoises into the constraint set. We learn this function from binary clean-sample evaluations alone, by squared-error regression on forward-noised labels; the base model is frozen, one lightweight head is trained per constraint, and noisy-state classifier guidance arises as a special case. The exact guidance step fades where the constraint signal provably vanishes and carries a factor of the inverse probability across samples, which normalized guidance discards: with the schedule and mean step size held fixed, equalizing the step costs 17.0 to 18.5 points of constraint satisfaction on CIFAR-10 at comparable FID, across independently trained estimators. Guidance is more than 50$\times$ cheaper per satisfying sample than rejection sampling at a 1.7% base rate, raises a Lipinski-type property filter on QM9 from 54.3% to 96.8%, and lifts satisfaction on Stable Diffusion 1.5 from 7.2% to 60.0% at one sixteenth of the cost of derivative-free selection, which reaches 9.0%. These results demonstrate that binary evaluations of clean samples are sufficient supervision for constrained generation across pixel, latent, and molecular diffusion.

title: Learning Gaussian Process Priors with Linear Semigroups and Kinetic Regularisation
summary: We introduce a semigroup-based construction of Gaussian process (GP) priors. A linear semigroup transforms a source GP at $t=0$ into a prior at $t=1$, enabling computationally tractable regression. Linearity preserves Gaussianity, allowing us to characterise the evolution of the covariance and draw connections with optimal transport and convolution models. The semigroup is parametrised by its generator, which is learned through two competing objectives: the marginal likelihood encourages agreement with observations, while a kinetic-energy regulariser favours lower-energy trajectories and limits unnecessary mass displacement from the source GP. Experiments on independent GP draws show that, with sufficiently many training functions, the learned prior provides accurate predictions on held-out functions, while kinetic regularisation substantially reduces the energy of the generated trajectories without compromising prediction accuracy.

title: Information-Theoretic Analysis of Multi-Objective Bandits: Pareto Violations & Gap-Based Regret
summary: We study Bayesian multi-objective bandits and ask an information-theoretic question: what aspects of an unknown environment must be resolved to achieve low regret? We show that the answer depends on the regret criterion and the information needed to represent its loss. For Pareto-violation regret, which incurs unit loss whenever a dominated action is selected, the Pareto-optimal set is a natural information target. We introduce a predictive separation measure for competing candidate Pareto sets, connect it to information gain about the unknown set, and use this connection to analyze Thompson Sampling and develop an Information-Directed Sampling strategy. We establish sublinear Bayesian regret under uniform and polynomially decaying separation and prove a lower bound showing that weak separation can impose an unavoidable statistical cost. We then study gap-based Pareto regret, which quantifies the magnitude of Pareto suboptimality. Here, Pareto-set information is generally too coarse: distinct environments can share the same Pareto set while inducing different reward geometries and Pareto gaps, and averaging environments consistent with one Pareto set need not preserve Pareto dominance. This motivates retaining finer information about the environment. We develop parameter-level information-theoretic analyses of Thompson Sampling and Information-Directed Sampling to derive gap-based regret guarantees. Under sublinear information budgets, Pareto Thompson Sampling also achieves sublinear gap regret while recovering the full Pareto set on the same run, with a related guarantee for a fixed mixture with gap-based IDS. Together, our results reveal a hierarchy of information requirements: binary Pareto membership can be controlled through set-level information, whereas quantitative Pareto-gap suboptimality can require finer knowledge of reward geometry.

title: Model Immunization Cannot Reliably Protect Models from Harmful Adaptation
summary: Efficient fine-tuning techniques have substantially reduced the cost of adapting open-weight models, enabling malicious actors to readily fine-tune them toward harmful capabilities. In response, model immunization modifies a pretrained checkpoint to resist subsequent adaptation toward designated harmful capabilities while preserving its utility and adaptability for benign tasks. Furthermore, a few immunization methods have sought to keep their protection robust to some changes in the attacker's adaptation. However, fine-tuning offers attackers many more low-cost options, and we observe that existing methods still substantially overfit to the attacker configuration they are optimized against. Such overfitting stays hidden when immunization is evaluated under, or near, this configuration, so the reported protection may give a false sense of security. To rigorously evaluate model immunization, we conduct experiments, varying one component of this configuration at a time: the harmful data, the adaptation strategy, or the model initialization. Across four immunization methods on text-to-image generation and image classification, with additional results on language models, these variations substantially degrade the protection, and in many cases the immunized model relearns the harmful capability nearly as well as the un-immunized model. Existing immunization therefore cannot reliably protect models, leaving them vulnerable to harmful adaptation.

title: When Source-Domain Validation Fails to Transfer: A Staged Study of Hyperparameter Selection
comment: 25 pages, 2 figures. Expanded version of work accepted to the AAAI-27 Student Abstract and Poster Program
summary: Hyperparameters for an unseen domain are often selected using held-out examples from the available source domains. Withholding entire source domains during validation seems to better reflect deployment shift, but does this produce better selections on independent targets? We investigate this question through two complementary studies. A preliminary factorial experiment crosses particle swarm optimization and random search with pooled source validation and a leave-one-source-domain-out mean-minimum fitness on PACS and Multi-Domain Sentiment. The domain-aware fitness does not provide a consistent target advantage. We then separate selector development from confirmation using a shared pool of 64 configurations per task across four image benchmarks. Complete target-performance landscapes on VLCS and Office-Home inform one rule: retain the top 16 configurations by pooled source validation, then select the largest leave-one-source-domain-out mean-minus-standard-deviation score. The rule is frozen before evaluation on TerraIncognita and SVIRO. Across their 14 target domains, its equal-dataset-weighted balanced-accuracy difference from pooled validation is +0.097 percentage points (95% bootstrap interval [-0.685, +0.960]), with five wins and nine losses. Exploratory analyses reveal substantial variation across datasets, target domains, and training seeds. These results do not establish equivalence or a general failure of domain-aware validation. They show that the evaluated source-domain criteria did not establish reliable target gains under the tested protocols, and motivate assessing selection rules on datasets independent of those used to develop them.

title: World Models Are the Right Foundation for Simulating Mars Terraforming
summary: Terraforming Mars is a long-horizon, action-conditioned control problem that requires predicting atmospheric responses to interventions over centuries to identify effective policies. This position paper argues that physics-regularized recurrent state-space world models are the most promising foundation for this setting. Data-driven climate emulators lack action-conditioning, and physics-based general circulation models (GCMs) are too expensive for policy search. Among learned world models, recurrent state-space architectures with physics constraints are better suited than transformer-based alternatives: they provide native uncertainty quantification through their stochastic-deterministic decomposition, remain stable under sparse non-terrestrial training data, and enforce physical consistency at each rollout step. To make this position concrete, we describe a potential architecture combining JEPA-inspired latent encoding, universal differential equation constraints, and a Dreamer-lineage planning head. We also introduce MarsWorld, an open benchmark proposal for intervention-conditioned planetary world models, and discuss broader implications and objections.

title: Safe Quantum Stochastic Linear Bandits
summary: We initiate the study of safe quantum stochastic linear bandits, in which a learner maximizes an unknown linear reward while satisfying unknown linear mean constraints at every interaction. Under coherent unitary access to the joint reward-and-constraint distribution, we develop QRS-COLTS, a staged quantum resampled-scaling analog of constrained linear Thompson sampling (COLTS). With high probability, QRS-COLTS plays only feasible actions and achieves regret that is polylogarithmic in the query horizon and scales only with the square root of the number of constraints. We also study a model in which the learner queries superpositions of actions while an unsafe-action flag, a "bomb" that terminates the interaction upon violation, is measured after every query. In this setting, the bomb provides exact membership access to the safe set, and query regret is evaluated over the action superposition. For this model, we propose BCO-QLinTS, which selects feasible actions via bomb-certified quantum convex optimization without estimating the constraint matrix. Its query-weighted regret remains polylogarithmic in the horizon, with the constraints entering the bound only through the geometry of the safe set.

title: Bridging the Gap between Continual Learning and Test-Time Adaptation with Domain Preview
summary: Domain shift is a major problem for training machine learning models. While Continual Learning (CL) assumes distribution shift during training and Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) considers new domains at test time, setups that require explicit online adaptation to domain shift during both phases remain under-explored. We propose continual learning with domain preview (CL-P), a new combination of CL and TTA where both train and test data suffer from distribution shift. The training phase of CL-P is analogous to domain-incremental learning while the testing phase consists of a TTA phase on a future domain (which we call preview), and an evaluation phase on all seen domains. The model must then adapt to new domains at train and test time. In this paper, we evaluate mainstream CL and TTA methods that adapt only at train or test time, as well as their naive combination. Experimentally, TTA heavily damages the domain on which the CL method has just trained and increases forgetting. Notably, this damage mostly comes from the BatchNorm statistics shared by all domains. In that sense, we propose DOSE (Dosing by Online Statistics of Each domain), which allows a seamless combination of any CL and TTA methods by adaptive domain inference at test time, where the adaptation is applied to each image in proportion to the probability that it comes from the preview domain. Through extensive experiments with ResNet and ViT backbones, various combinations of CL and TTA baseline methods and datasets considering diverse domains, we show that DOSE matches or improves on CL methods alone in all 24 settings and on the naive combination in all but one. The code can be found in appendix.

title: Beyond PINNs: Boundary-Enriched Holomorphic Networks for Laplace Problems
comment: Accepted at the AI for Science Workshop, NeurIPS 2026. 24 pages, 9 figures
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) solve partial differential equations by penalizing their residual, but this formulation can be difficult to optimize for solutions with singular behaviour. We focus specifically on the two-dimensional Laplace equation, whose strong analytical structure allows the governing equation to be enforced directly in the neural representation. We compare a hybrid harmonic-neural model with a holomorphic neural network whose output is harmonic by construction and therefore requires only boundary training. We further enrich the holomorphic model with singular functions chosen according to the interior angle and boundary conditions at each junction of boundary segments. On six singular benchmarks, the enriched model is the most accurate of the neural models we compare. On the four with a closed-form solution, however, that solution lies in the span of the enrichment terms, and a least-squares fit of these terms alone is exact to rounding error. On Motz's problem and the cracked beam, the neural core reduces the relative error of the recovered leading singular coefficient from about $10^{-2}$, for a least-squares fit with the same four terms, to about $10^{-6}$, and on four variants whose solution has a smooth part outside the span, the network is $4\times10^{4}$ to $2\times10^{7}$ times more accurate than a fit of its singular terms alone; classical least-squares fits with more singular terms, or with harmonic polynomials and rational poles, are more accurate still. Our results demonstrate how exploiting problem-specific analytical structure can provide an alternative to base and residual PINNs for challenging scientific computing problems.

title: Beyond Fixed Prompt Configuration: Alternating Policy Learning for Adaptive Topology-Based Prompting in Few-Shot Graph Learning
summary: Graph Prompt Learning (GPL) adapts frozen pre-trained graph models to few-shot graph tasks through a small set of trainable prompts that encode task-specific information. Topology-based prompting instantiates this idea by augmenting an input graph with new prompt nodes and edges, yielding promising performance. However, prompt content and propagation structure are coupled, making it difficult to assess their individual effects and learn compatible configurations. In this paper, we empirically analyze two challenges in learning adaptive policies for topology-based prompting: asymmetric performance effects and coupled configuration selection. We then propose TTPR, a two-stage reinforcement framework that alternately optimizes two policies to generate adaptive configurations, with each policy conditioned on configurations generated by the other fixed policy. These conditional updates separate policy evaluation while preserving configuration compatibility. Specifically, TTPR models an edge-level policy to construct connection patterns and optimizes it with Connection Relative Policy Optimization (CRPO) through group-wise comparisons of complete connection patterns. The other is a node-level policy that generates prompt-node schemes and is optimized with Incremental Node Proximal Policy Optimization (INPPO) through incremental prompt-count decisions and feature generation. Across diverse datasets and pre-training strategies, TTPR ranks first in 8/10 few-shot node classification settings and attains the highest average performance across graph classification benchmarks.

title: Yggdrasil: Tree-Routed Recurrent Experts for State Tracking and Fast CPU Inference
summary: Parallel-trainable recurrences such as Mamba, linear attention, and DeltaNet offer constant-cost streaming inference, but they suffer from two limitations: 1) they struggle to track discrete state, and 2) they read every parameter at every step, tying model capacity directly to CPU latency. We introduce Yggdrasil, a recurrent architecture that decouples capacity from per-step compute by looking up each layer's transition in a large, tree-routed bank of recurrent experts. Each router addresses its bank using the current token and the state of the layer below. We prove that this cross-layer context is necessary---a single token-indexed layer of non-expanding transitions with finitely many reachable states cannot perform conditional resets---while avoiding feedback from the layer's own past preserves parallel-scan training. Because each step traverses one tree path and reads a single expert per layer, active weights stay within a few hundred kilobytes in CPU L2 cache while the full bank resides in RAM. Among the parallel-trainable models we evaluate, Yggdrasil is the only one to solve all five state-tracking tasks. At matched active parameter counts, it achieves the lowest test bits on enwik8 (1.540 bpb) and the human genome hg38 (1.567 bpb), while stepping $3.0\times$ and $3.3\times$ faster on a single CPU core ($6.7\,μ\mathrm{s}$ and $5.8\,μ\mathrm{s}$) than the fastest streaming baseline, and delivering the highest GPU throughput of all models at batch 1024. On the Genomic Benchmarks, it is the strongest causal model at matched active parameters (86.0% mean accuracy).

title: Tracing Attacker Diversity Reduction in Adaptive LLM Red Teaming
summary: Reinforcement learning can increase the success of automated red teaming but it also narrows the attack vector. This study asks where in the attacker-defender-judge learning loop does the narrowing begin and which mechanisms lead to a narrowing attack. Six mechanisms (defender adaptation, success edge, reward reinforcement, row cap, update size, and measurement) are tested across three experiment arms (co-trained, frozen defender, half learning rate) for twenty-four iterations. A frozen defender narrows attack diversity retention (ADR) earlier 0.496 relative to co-trained 0.891 at iteration twelve. Defender updates delay narrowing but dont prevent it. Successful attacks ("winners") have narrower attack diversity than the full set of generated attacks. Attacks closest to previous winners succeed 10-15 percentage points more often than those closest to previous failures. This winner-neighbor advantage holds after a defender update and for a fixed defender too. Attacks with a common opening have a common-opening advantage of 5-16 percentage points. The training row cap and update size account for little impact on ADR, and attack length accounts for only part of the ADR decrease. Narrowing appears to originate from the success only reward through the group-relative training advantage to the attacker update, with a persistent success edge setting the direction.

title: Training Dynamics of Large State-Transition Models
summary: Next-token prediction relies on learned token embeddings whose dimension $d$ is much smaller than the vocabulary size $V$. Existing analyses of training dynamics either fix the embeddings with $d\ge V$ or train them only in restricted settings. It remains unclear whether jointly training the embeddings by gradient-based methods from random initialization leads to accurate prediction when $d<V$. In this paper, we study this question in the simplest setting where it is already nontrivial, namely next-token prediction with a one-token context, which we refer to as a state-transition model. The model consists of an input embedding and an output embedding, either untied or tied, and is trained from Gaussian initialization by perturbed gradient descent with weight decay on the population cross-entropy loss. We consider ground-truth transition laws whose centered log-probability table has low rank and bounded entries, and measure the prediction quality by the relative prediction gain (RPG). It is zero for the uniform predictor and one for the optimal predictor. For the untied model, we show that when $d=Ω(\sqrt V)$, with probability at least $1-e^{-cd}$ for some constant $c$, the RPG is above $7/8$ at every iterate in the final $1-1/d$ fraction of training iterations. For the tied model trained on a subset of states, we prove that the RPG on the observed states is $1-O(V/d^2)$, and under a coverage condition on the ground truth and a bound on the learned embeddings, we further prove a prediction guarantee on the unseen states. Our analysis is based on the bounded trace of the Hessian of the softmax cross-entropy loss, which implies that the approximate second-order stationary points reached by training have high prediction gain. Numerical experiments with practical parameter choices illustrate the persistent training gain and the transfer of the tied model.

title: Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neurons (DAWIN): A Universal Primitive for Continuous-Time Spatiotemporal Learning
summary: Conventional artificial neurons separate spatial feature aggregation from continuous physical time, limiting their ability to model irregular observations. We introduce the Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neuron (DAWIN), a continuous-time primitive for replacing standard neural layers in MLPs, Transformers, and graph neural networks. DAWIN couples spatial projection with elapsed-time-dependent wave excitation and integrates it into a local complex state through closed-form damped evolution, avoiding numerical differential equation solvers. We show that DAWIN generalizes static sinusoidal and memoryless wave neurons on interval-augmented inputs, derive closed-form gradients, and establish bounded-input bounded-output stability for positive damping and sampling intervals bounded away from zero. An associative Triton prefix-scan implementation, DAWINLinear, uses FP32 accumulation and achieves O(log L) parallel depth for sequence length L. Across 11 parameter-matched tasks covering irregular oscillators, MuJoCo dynamics, pedestrian trajectories, and PhysioNet 2012 clinical sequences, DAWIN outperforms Neural CDE on 9 tasks and ReLU-MLP on 8. It achieves the lowest error on dense clinical dynamics (0.9531 NRMSE, winning across all 10 seeds) and ties for the best mortality prediction (0.9993 AUROC). Shuffling elapsed intervals increases error by 58.2%-77.4% on selected dynamics tasks, versus 0.06% on a time-irrelevant control, supporting reliance on physical timing. On NVIDIA B200 GPUs, parallel wave integration accelerates inference by up to 2,630 times over its serial implementation and reduces peak GPU memory by up to 97.6% relative to Mamba in the tested configurations.

title: Fast 4-bit KV-Cache Decoding on Hopper GPUs: Why Existing Kernels Are Slow and How to Fix Them
summary: A 4-bit KV cache reads about half the bytes of FP8, but Hopper GPUs have no FP4 hardware and little instruction-issue capacity per byte of memory bandwidth, so 4-bit values must be decoded in software. On H200, vLLM's NVFP4 KV path (FlashInfer's decode) reaches 10-20% of memory bandwidth and is up to 1.7x slower than FP8. NVBit instruction counts show two causes: the kernels behind vLLM's 4-bit paths (FlashInfer NVFP4, Triton UltraQuant) execute 2-6x Hopper's issue budget per byte and serialize loading, decoding and matrix multiplies. Our Hopper-native decode kernel overlaps a TMA producer warp with two compute warpgroups, lays the cache out at write time so decoded values feed the tensor cores from registers, and swaps the matrix operands so small query groups need no padding. On H200 it reaches 67-75% of peak bandwidth at batch 32-128 and at all 11 shapes is 1.12-1.49x faster than the faster of XQA and FlashAttention-4's proposed native FP8. Inside vLLM, with an accuracy recipe (K mean removal and rotation, 4 BF16 sink tokens, BF16 layer 0), it decodes 1.12-1.64x faster per step on Llama-3.1-8B than vLLM's FlashInfer FP8 path at batch 8 and above (1.04-1.24x over FlashAttention-4's FP8), is level at batch 1, and holds 1.63x as many tokens. On one H200 under a reasoning-like request stream, the highest rate at which 99% of requests meet the latency targets is 1.23-1.32x FP8's on Llama-3.1-8B and 1.67-2.20x on Qwen2.5-72B, as the cache becomes the limit; prefill-heavy streams are worse (7% slower prefill). On five 7B-32B models, repeated runs show no significant accuracy difference from BF16 KV. In Qwen2-family models, whose reasoning variants collapse under FP8 KV, layer 0's key mean is almost entirely the key-projection bias identified by prior work, seen through RoPE and computable from the weights alone; keeping that layer in BF16 restores FP8 KV and, with K mean removal, 4-bit KV.

title: PsyDrift: Healthy-Reference Latent Diffusion for Anomaly Scoring in Autism Spectrum Disorder
comment: Extended version of a paper accepted at the CVPath-Vision4Neuro Workshop at WACV 2027. Includes expanded related-work and future-work discussion
summary: Individual heterogeneity and acquisition-site variability complicate neuroimaging-based characterization of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We propose PsyDrift, combining ASD/healthy-control-supervised functional-connectivity representations with healthy-reference latent diffusion. An encoder produces 128-dimensional representations, and a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) learns exclusively from healthy training latents. Distance from a diffusion-denoised reconstruction provides a continuous deviation score. We evaluate 1,102 subjects from all 20 ABIDE-I sites using five-seed leave-one-site-out cross-validation. The classifier and DDPM achieve mean-site AUROCs of $0.798 \pm 0.003$ and $0.718 \pm 0.013$, respectively; uncertainties denote seed standard deviations. Matched healthy-reference scorers on the same representation achieve 0.68-0.71; the statistical significance of diffusion's modest numerical advantage remains unestablished. Within ASD, scores show weak associations with ADOS Total (Spearman $ρ= 0.108$, $p = 0.038$) and full-scale IQ ($ρ= -0.138$, $p = 0.002$), without adjustment for age, sex, site, or head motion. Frozen evaluation without retraining or hyperparameter adaptation yields pooled AUROCs of 0.69 on ABIDE-II and 0.61 on ADHD-200, providing preliminary evidence of cross-cohort and cross-disorder transfer. These results demonstrate healthy-reference deviation scoring within an ASD-supervised representation; incremental predictive and clinical value remains unestablished.

title: How Latent Transition Geometry Matters for Planning in World Models
summary: World models support planning by predicting how the environment evolves under candidate actions. However, one-step predictive accuracy alone does not characterize multi-step planning utility, which depends on distinguishing candidate futures.
